BrightGrid Solar Net-Metering Policy:
- Customers with rooftop solar generating more energy than consumed in a billing cycle receive a credit at the full retail rate for the first 500 kWh of excess, and at the wholesale rate (roughly 40% of retail) for any excess beyond 500 kWh in that same cycle.
- Credits roll over month to month and never expire, but are forfeited if the account is closed rather than paid out in cash.
- A one-time "true-up" reconciliation happens every 12 months, at which point any rolled-over credit balance worth more than $500 is paid out as a check; balances at or under $500 simply continue rolling over.

Account #77021 solar summary, August billing cycle: consumed 620 kWh, generated 950 kWh, for an excess of 330 kWh this cycle. Rolling credit balance carried in from before this cycle: 410 kWh, worth $61.50 at blended historical rates. This is month 11 since the account's last true-up.

Customer's message: "Hi, doing my annual review of the solar credits since we're coming up on the anniversary of our system going live. Based on my own tracking, this month's excess should be under the 500 kWh full-retail-rate cap, so it should all credit at the higher rate, unlike a couple of summer months last year where we blew past 500 and some of it got the lower wholesale rate. Can you confirm this month's number, and let me know what happens at the 12-month true-up next month if my rolled-over balance is still under $500 by then -- do I still get a check, or does it just keep rolling since it's under the threshold?"

Account specialist's internal note, added after pulling the full 12-month history: Customer's system has generated excess in 9 of the last 11 months, with only two months (both this past July and August of last year) exceeding the 500 kWh cap, each by a modest margin that pushed a small portion of that month's credit to the wholesale rate. No true-up has occurred yet on this account since installation, so next month's cycle will be the very first one. Current rolled-over balance of $61.50 is well within normal range for a system of this size at this point in its first year, based on comparable accounts in the same service area. Specialist recommends replying with a plain-language walkthrough of both numbers (this month's rate split and the true-up mechanics) rather than just a one-line confirmation, since the customer's message shows they've clearly done their own homework and would likely appreciate the detail rather than a generic answer.

NimbleBank Identity Theft Resolution Policy:
- New accounts opened fraudulently in a customer's name are closed at no cost within 5 business days of a filed police report or FTC identitytheft.gov report.
- Existing account takeovers (unauthorized access to an account the customer already had) follow the standard fraud dispute process instead, with provisional credit rules, not the identity-theft account-closure process.
- Both processes can run in parallel if a customer experiences both an account takeover AND a new fraudulent account in the same incident.

Customer's message: "This is a mess. Someone got into my existing checking account and moved $600 out via a transfer I didn't authorize, AND I just found out through a credit alert that a new NimbleBank credit card was opened in my name that I never applied for. I filed a police report yesterday and have the report number ready to share. What happens with each of these, are they handled the same way or differently? I'd like both dealt with as soon as possible given the amounts involved."

Fraud team's intake note, logged the same day: Verified the police report number against the local department's online case lookup, confirms a report was indeed filed yesterday under this customer's name matching the details described. Existing checking account transfer of $600 has been flagged and provisional credit rules now apply per standard dispute procedure while the transfer itself is investigated with the receiving institution. New credit card application under this customer's name and SSN was submitted three days ago through an online channel; account has been placed on hold pending closure once the 5-business-day clock referenced in policy runs, with the clock starting from today's report. Customer will receive separate case numbers for each track so progress on one is never confused with the other. Given the combined dollar amount and the same-day request for urgency, this case has also been flagged internally for priority handling rather than the standard queue, with a specialist assigned to personally monitor both tracks until closure.

BeautyLoot Mid-Cycle Plan Change Policy:
- Upgrading mid-cycle (for example, Classic to Deluxe): the customer is charged a prorated difference for the remaining days in the current cycle, calculated as (price difference / 30) multiplied by days remaining.
- Downgrading mid-cycle: no refund for the difference; the lower price simply takes effect next cycle.
- Cancelling mid-cycle: no partial refund for days remaining in the current cycle; the plan runs through the already-paid period.

Case: Classic plan is $24/month, Deluxe is $39/month, a $15 difference. The customer upgraded from Classic to Deluxe on day 10 of a 30-day cycle, leaving 20 days remaining in the cycle.

Customer's message: "Hi, I just upgraded to Deluxe from the app and it charged me $15 right away -- can you confirm that's the prorated amount for the days left this cycle and not some separate new fee? The math based on what I could find on your help page suggests it should be $15 times 20 over 30, which comes out to $10, not $15, so now I'm second-guessing myself. Can you clarify which number is actually right?"

Billing engineer's note, pulled after the customer's message came in: Reviewed the proration function in the upgrade service and found a rounding-and-fees bug introduced three weeks ago in release v4.12 -- the function is currently adding a flat $5 "tier change processing fee" on top of the correctly calculated prorated amount, which explains the $10 versus $15 discrepancy exactly ($10 correct proration plus the erroneous $5 equals the $15 actually charged). This processing fee was never part of the published mid-cycle policy and was not intentionally introduced; it appears to be leftover test code that shipped by mistake. Engineering has been notified and a fix is scheduled, but in the meantime any customer who upgraded since v4.12 shipped should have the $5 difference refunded manually until the fix goes out. Support lead's follow-up note: pulled a list of all upgrades since v4.12 shipped three weeks ago, 214 accounts affected in total, refund batch scheduled to run tonight so most customers won't even need to ask, this customer's message just happened to arrive a few hours ahead of that batch job. Recommend replying today anyway to acknowledge the question directly, rather than letting the customer wonder if their message went unnoticed just because the fix and refund happen to already be in motion behind the scenes.

MarketLoop Counterfeit Goods Policy:
- Buyers with a credible, substantiated counterfeit claim (for example, manufacturer verification denying a serial number) receive a full refund AND are not required to return the item, since counterfeit goods cannot be resold and returning them may be illegal to ship in some jurisdictions.
- Sellers found to have sold counterfeit goods in 2 or more substantiated claims are permanently banned from the platform.
- A single unsubstantiated "I think this might be fake" claim with no supporting evidence is treated as a standard not-as-described case instead, requiring the normal return process.

Buyer's claim on order #90341: "I bought what was listed as an authentic LumeTech smartwatch. I contacted LumeTech's official support with the serial number and they confirmed in writing, screenshot attached, that this serial number was never issued by them at all, meaning it's confirmed counterfeit, not just something that looks a little off to me personally. This is the seller's third substantiated counterfeit claim this year according to the case history notes I can see on my end. I'd like a refund, and I'd also like to know if I even need to send this back given it's apparently not a real product in the first place."

Trust & safety case history, visible to the reviewing agent: Claim #1 against this seller (Jan): substantiated counterfeit claim on a different smartwatch model, manufacturer confirmed invalid serial number, refund issued, item not required to be returned per policy. Claim #2 (May): substantiated counterfeit claim on a phone charger listed as an official accessory, manufacturer confirmed it was never part of their authorized product line, refund issued. Claim #3 (this case, September): manufacturer-confirmed invalid serial number on a smartwatch, screenshot of LumeTech's written response attached by the buyer. All three claims involve independent manufacturer verification rather than buyer speculation, meeting the policy's definition of "substantiated" each time. Trust & safety lead's recommendation: process this buyer's refund immediately without requiring a return label, and open a formal seller-ban review given this is now the third confirmed instance within the same calendar year, which crosses the policy's two-claim threshold for permanent removal from the platform. Noting for the file that this seller was given a warning after claim #2 in May rather than an immediate ban, since policy language at the time was ambiguous about whether two claims meant an automatic ban or a discretionary review; that ambiguity has since been clarified in favor of an automatic ban at two or more, which is why this third claim now triggers it without further discretion needed.
